If statistics are correct that one in ten men are gay, then which one of the twelve disciples of Christ was gay? One of them had to be a closet case. That’s not how probabilities work. Taking your statistic at face value, the probability that at least one of the 12 disciples was gay would be calculated as: 1 − ( 1 − p ) n 1 − ( 1 – 1 10 ) 12 71.8 % And sure, 71.8% is decently high odds, but it’s not guaranteed that “One of them had to be a closet case.” Take in other potential objections, such as whether or not that stat truly is accurate, or whether folks 2000 years ago even had the same conceptions of gay vs. straight as we do today, and it’s problematic to try to draw any conclusions around this.

Will drinking beer while still on a calorie deficit affect my fat loss? As the old saying goes – everything in moderation. If you don't drink in moderation, it can be a real whammy to weight loss. First you get all the calories from the beer itself. Beer can range anywhere from around 100 calories for an American light lager to over 300 calories for a Belgian triple. Drink a bunch of craft beers and IPAs for a night on the town with friends, and that could add up to a few thousand calories worth of beer alone. Then, you get the munchies that come along with that, combined with the lower inhibitions caused by the alcohol, and that 3 am trip to the drive thru (with your DD driving, of course) to pick up a double bacon cheeseburger with a large fries sounds like just the thing. Then you've got the hangover the next day, with yet more cravings for greasy fried foods, just adding to the calories. In short, aside from any of the other reasons to avoid overdoing it with beer, you definitely don't want to do so if you're trying to lose weight. But if you do stick to moderation, you should be fine. The key to losing weight is to consume less calories than you expend, and you don't need to stick to diet food to achieve that goal. I myself lost around 60 lbs by eating a normal balanced diet, just less of it. And yes, I still treated myself to occasional desserts and sweets, and usually a few beers over the weekend. Complete abstinence just leads to temptation.

Are there any fossil remains of the fish that decided to walk onto land, thus becoming a man? Yes, but a couple clarifications, first. First, it's not like any fish personally decided to grow limbs that were closer to legs than fins. Mutation really is a random process beyond the conscious control of the organisms experiencing those mutations. Just think about yourself. Did you choose any of the genetic mutations that differentiate you from your parents? If you have any children, did you choose any of the genetic mutations that got passed on to them? No, of course not. Such mutations are things that happen on a chemical level that we're never aware of. Heck, us people are just about the only organisms with the smarts to even understand genetics in the first place, so our ancient fish ancestors certainly weren't thinking about genetic mutations. Second, evolution of such big transitions is a gradual process that takes many, many generations to happen. It's not like there was a fish species that instantly evolved into a land dwelling animal, let alone into us humans. There were many stages along the way, from 'walking' underwater (similar to frogfish or certain walking sharks in the modern day), to slightly amphibious lifestyles (like some catfish), to even more amphibious lifestyles (like mudskippers), to something that's finally fully specialized for a life totally on land. Here's a diagram showing some of the stages along the fish to tetrapod transition, with some extra detail on the limbs, and how these limbs gradually went through this transition from fully aquatic to amphibious to fully terrestrial: ABOVE SOURCE: The origin of tetrapods Here's another figure to give a sense of the transition from those first tetrapods to us people. One thing that can sometimes be a bit misleading about diagrams like this is showing just a single path, perhaps giving the impression that this path was inevitably leading towards us. But you could make diagrams like this for any living creature, e.g. the path to mosquitos, the path to dandelions, or the path to a mushroom. And even in this path, at any critter on there, if you weren't specifically interested in human evolution, you could go off in a different direction to look at other creatures. For example, from Orrorin around 6 million years ago, you could go down a different path that led to chimpanzees rather than us people. Or from that Repenomamus around 230 million years ago, you could pick paths to any mammal alive today. ABOVE SOURCE: Visualized: The 4 Billion Year Path of Human Evolution And just to be clear, all of the animals shown in both of those figures are known from fossil remains, sometimes more than one specimen for each species. Just going with the first figure, here are some of the available fossils: ABOVE: Eusthenopteron SOURCE: File:Eusthenopteron foordi 1.jpg - Simple English Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia ABOVE: Panderichthys SOURCE: Panderichthys | Fossiilid.info ABOVE: Tiktaalik SOURCE: Famous fish fossil takes final bow in Philadelphia ABOVE: Acanthostega SOURCE: File:Acanthostega Deep Time.jpg - Wikimedia Commons ABOVE: Ichthyostega SOURCE: Ichthyostega Fossil Skeleton, First Fish to grow legs & move onto land ABOVE: Tulerpeton (I couldn't find an actual photo in a quick Google search, but this at least shows which bones were actually found – in white, and which are only inferred – in grey) SOURCE: Tulerpeton curtum by Ivanbel on DeviantArt

I totally believe the evolution theory because it has tons of scientific evidence, but I don't get it how marine life evolved to have lungs, limbs, developed, and somehow intelligent brain to live on land? I think part of the problem is people only think about a stereotypical, generic fish, and don't know about or don't think about the wide variety we see in living fish. You mentioned lungs and limbs, so let's take a look at those. And let's start with the limbs, since it makes for cooler videos. First, here's a frogfish. To be clear, frogfish aren't particularly closely related to the first tetrapods. They're adapted to a fully aquatic lifestyle without ever venturing onto land. But yet, they walk underwater, because it's a better way for them to get around, and especially to use their fins to sit on the ocean floor waiting to ambush prey. And here's a type of walking shark. Again, these are fully aquatic sharks. Their walking isn't some type of planning ahead for a life on the land, but a very useful means of locomotion to prowl around a reef. Next, let's move on to lungs. Air breathing is in fact quite common in many lineages of fish. Oxygen is much more consistent in the atmosphere than in the water, so many fish will surface to swallow gulps of air. Somewhere around 400 million years ago, the common ancestor of bony fish evolved a primitive lung as an outgrowth of the stomach as a way to improve oxygen absorption from these swallowed gulps. Over time, some lineages developed more advanced lungs, while others actually went in a different direction, and the lung evolved into a swim bladder. It just so happens that the lineage that evolved a swim bladder has gone on to become the most successful lineage of fish, so it somewhat biases our perception of what's normal. But a look at the bony fish family tree shows lungs to be rather widespread: ABOVE: The lineages in solid black still have lungs, while the lineages with the dashed outlines evolved swim bladders. SOURCE: How did fish evolve the ability to breathe on land? But even in the lineages that traded lungs for swim bladders, in certain environments, it's still beneficial for fish to be able to breathe air, and so various lineages have evolved new adaptations to allow this. Some fish, like bettas, are so dependent on atmospheric oxygen that they'll 'drown' if they can't get to the surface to take a breath. ABOVE SOURCE: Accessory Respiratory Organs of Fishes (With Diagram) | Chordata | Zoology So, just looking at living species of fish, walking and breathing air are relatively common. And from there, it's not a big step (get it?) to begin spending some time on land. Even that is common enough in living fish, from mudskippers to walking catfish to another species of walking shark that I didn't show here (Epaulette Shark Walks on Land). And once you have fish spending some time on land, well, it's not hard to see how they could become even more specialized to spend even more time on land. In other words, there's no need to ponder any special or unique conditions for why our ancestors would have evolved legs or lungs to make the transition from water to land, since we see plenty of analogs in fish alive right now. They’re simply useful features for some fish to have.

Why do most Americans prefer processed food and artificial over fresh and natural food? Because ‘processing’ isn’t the boogey man you think it is. Processed foods are delicious. And in many cases, the processing actually makes the foods safer and more nutritious. ABOVE SOURCE: The Truth About Eating Processed Foods — The Bodybuilding Dietitians Let me give an example. I like milk and dairy products. Only one time in my life have I I tried unprocessed milk, right after milking it from the cow. It was even still warm. But most of the time, I buy my milk from the grocery store, so I want it pasteurized to make sure it's safe from pathogens. I also like cheese and butter, which are both also processed foods (they're no longer simply raw milk). And for a lot of folks, the processing to make cheese or yogurt can reduce the lactose for people who have issues with that. Same thing with bread. I could eat bread all day. Raw, unprocessed wheat? Not so much. The grinding and cooking even make the nutrients easier to digest. And meat? Now, don't get me wrong. There's nothing wrong with a steak that's only minimally processed (butchering, seasoning, and cooking). But sausages, ham, and bacon? Oh man. A world without bacon would be a sad world indeed. And maybe you think I'm being a smartass, but I'm not. I'm going to guess that you weren't considering bread to be a processed food, but it is. Some foods may be processed more than others, but it's hard to draw any clear dividing line between what's too processed and what isn't. I mean, how does extra chopping or mixing magically make foods unhealthy? I've got the same pet peeves over 'artificial' ingredients. We don't have Star Trek replicators that can create molecules from scratch from energy. Everything we put into our food came from nature at some point. Where do you draw the line between natural and artificial ingredients? And even if you do have some threshold of chemistry that you'll use to designate 'artificial' ingredients, what does that have to do with health or safety? (As an example from medicine, we synthesize acetylsalicylic acid for aspirin, because it actually has less side effects than the naturally occurring salicylic acid found in willow bark that inspired the medicine.) And don't get me started on the silly saying that if you can't pronounce an ingredient, don't eat it. Have you ever seen all the chemical constituents of an egg? Practically all food is a complex mix of lots and lots of hard to pronounce chemicals. Most of those chemicals are safe. Some aren't. But whether or not they're safe has no correlation to how easy they are to pronounce. ABOVE SOURCE: Ingredients of an All-Natural Egg So yeah. I like sausage and bread and ham and pasteurized milk and all types of other processed foods I can buy from the grocery store. I eat processed food because I'm not a wild animal. While I was looking for images for processed foods, I came across many figures where people try to add an extra category, of ‘ultra processed’. Here’s one that was especially silly: ABOVE SOURCE: ABOVE SOURCE: MailOnline's guide to tell ultra-processed food apart They called French fries ultra processed. Sliced potatoes fried in oil. I’m not sure how much less processing you can do to a cooked food. And they’ve got ice cream on there. My family had a hand cranked ice cream maker when I was growing up, and we used it quite a bit for extended family get togethers. It’s just milk, cream, sugar, and a little vanilla, mixed up in a container surrounded by ice and rock salt. What’s ‘ultra processed’ about that? Now, I’m not saying an excess of fries and ice cream would make a healthy diet, but it’s got nothing to do with the amount of processing that went into making them.

Do people with little animal door flaps ever get unwelcome intruders in their homes? More than once. A Midnight Visitor The first time was close to my daughter's 15th birthday. And I know that specifically because we had a full house of relatives who were in town for her quinceañera. Our doggie/cat door was from the house to the garage. We then left the small back door of the garage open to the back yard, so that the cats and weenie dog could get in and out that way. We'd occasionally had issues with racoons in the past when I kept the dog food out in the garage, but after I started securing the lid better, they started leaving us alone. But that evening, we'd left the big garage door open, and a family of racoons got into the garage. We thought we'd chased them all out, so we completely shut all the outside garage doors, thinking that would keep the entire family out. Sometime around two in the morning, the weenie dog started barking and barking, waking up everybody in the house. I came downstairs, and there he was, with a baby racoon cornered in the family room and a gathering crowd of family members. I guess one of the racoon family had been left behind and found its way through the doggie door. My uncle told me it was just a baby so why don't I just go and grab it. I shot back why doesn't he go grab it. In the end, we called animal control, and they came and got it. A Nosy Neighbor We went for years without any more unexpected visitors to the house. In the meantime, our previous cats and dogs had all died, and we'd become roommates with a new cat, who started off feral using our garage, and who I was able to eventually coax into the house and teach him how to use the cat door. My wife named him Chester. He was a long haired tabby cat. There was another long haired tabby cat running around the neighborhood who looked very similar. At first, I named this other cat Not Chester. But I eventually learned that he was an actual pet who belonged to our neighbor two houses down, who we then began calling Sir William Wallace the Gentleman. Well, being a house cat himself, he understood the concept of cat doors, and I began catching him, or evidence of him, in the house on a pretty regular basis. It was especially irritating to find the butter I left out on the counter with a whole bunch of cat sized bites taken out. The last straw was when I was in our upstairs office working from home, and he had the audacity to come all the way upstairs to the room I was in. After that, I investigated higher tech options, and bought an electronic cat flap that you could program to only unlock for your specific cat's RFID chip (which meant Chester also got a trip to the vet to get chipped). Problem solved, mostly. A Thief in the Night One problem with this cat flap is that the way it locked under normal operation, it only blocked the flap from opening inward. For going out, the flap could still swing open. This worked fine for most animals, but racoons aren't most animals. We had a container full of pecans in the dining room, close to the garage door, and I came down one morning to find pecan shells all over the dining room floor. I didn't think too much about it, and just cleaned them up. But when it happened again, I knew there was a problem. It seems that the racoon had figured out how to get just enough of a grip on the flap to pull it open from the outside. Somewhat fortuitously, that was just around the time I was getting ready to head to El Paso for a month, taking Chester with me. So I set the cat flap to the completely locked mode (which wouldn't open in either direction), and put a trash can right in front of it on the inside of the house. I think the racoon figured out that his free meal ticket was over, so that seemed to put an end to it. Still a Nosy Neighbor Now that we've had the electronic flap for a couple years, it doesn't swing quite as freely as it did when new. So sometimes when Chester comes in, it won't swing back all the way shut to where it gets locked. And so, just a month or two ago, I was downstairs with Chester on my lap, when I heard something eating his cat food. I looked, and there was Sir William Wallace stealing Chester's food. So I chased him out again. So yeah, we've had our share of uninvited guests thanks to the doggie/cat door. The electronic one seems to have solved most of the problems, but it hasn't stopped them completely.

Evolutionists have been debating the chicken and chicken egg question for a long time. Can evolution explain which came first? No, because evolution helps us to understand that it's not the type of thing you can pinpoint. It would be like trying to define the precise second when dusk becomes night, or the precise date that a child becomes an adult. It just doesn't work that way. These are gradual processes that elude precise demarcations. Evolution is a gradual accumulation of genetic changes within an entire population. In sexually reproducing animals, there's no single individual that's a different species from their parents, or indeed, the entire population of which they're a part. Plus, there's plenty of genetic variability within a population, which will be recombined in all types of different ways as the animals mate. So you can't even pick an individual organism as the first chicken, after which all of its descendants will subsequently be chickens, as that individual and its descendants will still have to mate with other members of the population, continuing to mix up those genes. Why did Tim Walz put female tampons and pads in the boys washroom? I have to say, this is one of the stranger tempests in a teapot I've seen in a while. The reality seems like such a mundane law (albeit very beneficial) that I’m surprised it’s managed to draw this much attention. But while most of the manufactured controversy came out of the right-wing, some left-wing responses have also been a bit more rationalization after the fact rather than what the law originally intended, and based more around conjecture than what's actually going on in Minnesota (i.e. it didn't have anything to do with logistics). So first – the civics lessons. Tim Walz didn't write this law. He didn't campaign on it or provide a draft for the legislature to act on. The law was originally sponsored by Sandra Feist in the Minnesota House, in a standalone bill, HF 44 , and then got included in the much larger Education Finance Bill, HF 2497. After going through the full process in the Minnesota House and Senate, the Education Finance Bill was eventually approved by majorities in both chambers, and so Tim Walz signed it into law. But this whole initiative of providing menstrual products to student was never something that Walz himself led. The main purpose of the law originally proposed by Feist is to provide menstrual products to students. This isn't some revolutionary idea new to Minnesota. There are similar laws on the books in 28 states and D.C. to address what some describe as "period poverty". According to Period Products in Schools, 1 in 4 students struggle to afford such products. And one study of a program in NYC found a 2.4% increase in attendance when free period products were offered to students. As one of the students who testified in the Minnesota House during a hearing on the legislation put it, "We cannot learn while we are leaking" (source: Minnesota may soon OK free menstrual products in schools. These teens led the way). ABOVE SOURCE: Period Products in Schools - Alliance for Period Supplies If you want to read the law for yourself, go to the full text of HF2497. It's easy to find the relevant portions. Just do a search for 'menstrual'. Here's the main portion: ARTICLE 1 GENERAL EDUCATION Section 1. [121A.212] ACCESS TO MENSTRUAL PRODUCTS. A school district or charter school must provide students with access to menstrual products at no charge. The products must be available to all menstruating students in restrooms regularly used by students in grades 4 to 12 according to a plan developed by the school district. For purposes of this section, "menstrual products" means pads, tampons, or other similar products used in connection with the menstrual cycle. There's another passage specifying that the budget for this will be "$2 times the adjusted pupil units of the school district for the school year", and another passage including these menstrual products in a list of allowed purposes for "Total operating capital revenue". Note that there's no mandate that tampons have to be supplied in the boys restroom. However, the language was gender neutral, allowing for discretion at the local levels for schools to implement this law. And that gender neutral language was on purpose. According to Feist, the sponsor of the original bill: While the vast majority of the period products will be used in the girls’ bathrooms, the decision was made to structure the bill as gender-inclusive in order to ensure that trans and nonbinary students who menstruate would have equal access to the products they need. SOURCE: Yes, Tim Walz signed a law requiring Minnesota public schools to provide free tampons in school bathrooms Also, as noted in the article, Why Republicans are calling Walz 'Tampon Tim' — and why Democrats embrace it, there was opposition to this gender inclusivity when "Some Minnesota Republicans initially tried to limit the initiative to female-assigned and gender-neutral bathrooms, but were unsuccessful." However, it's interesting to note that the Republican who proposed that amendment did go on to support the final bill, as he felt the overall issue was important, and not worth killing over that compromise. It’s also worth pointing out that schools are free to come up with their own plans to implement the law. According to an editorial from the Minnesota based Star Tribune, A reality check on the ‘Tampon Tim’ meme: At Anoka-Hennepin, the state’s largest school district, the free products are not found in traditional male-only bathrooms, a spokesman said. But they are provided for free to all in “nongendered bathrooms,” girls’ bathrooms or from health staffers. I can't say that absolutely no schools in Minnesota have provided tampons in the boys room, but if the largest school district in the state isn't doing so, it's obviously not a requirement of the law, so long as transgender students can still receive menstrual products if they need them. So basically, Tim Walz signed a large law that had a bunch of different sections dealing with multiple aspects of education funding. Among these was a requirement to provide tampons to students for free, which seems utterly reasonable to me. The language was made specifically gender neutral, allowing individual schools to implement the law as they saw fit, so long as they were still complying and supporting all students who needed menstrual products, which also seems pretty reasonable to me. And just to be clear, the law doesn't actually force schools to provide tampons in the boys room, and as proven in practice, at least one school district cited in the news hasn't.

What accidents or incidents have you personally had with deep fryers? Back when I was in high school, I got a job at KFC. There was a certain minimum level for the shortening in the pressure fryers, but they never actually gave us any formal training on proper technique to add more. The method I developed for myself was to cut off a chunk of shortening (it was solid at room temperature), then stab that chunk with the knife, and lower it down into the fryer. That seemed better to me than just throwing the chunk in there and having the hot grease splash. Well, one day, I had a just gotten a big chunk of shortening over the fryer when it fell off of the knife, and sent a huge splash of grease up at my head. I managed to turn to the side and close my eyes, but the grease got half of my face. I immediately went to the sink in the kitchen, and began running cold water over my face. The manager didn't seem to quite know what to do, and couldn't get a hold of my parents, so eventually, somebody gave me a ride home. When I did get home, my parents were out in the yard working (why they never heard the phone – this was a bit before cell phones), and were quite surprised to see me, especially with half my face burnt. So they immediately threw me into the car and drove me to the ER. The ER took me in right away (no waiting around like when you've merely got the sniffles), took me straight to a room, and then promptly treated me with nothing fancier than cold washcloths. Really, that was the only treatment – a basin of ice water with a few washcloths soaking in it, that my mom would swap out when the one on my face started to warm up too much. After a couple hours to draw out as much heat as possible, they sent me on my way with referrals for follow ups. Over the next few days, my face started to look bad. Luckily, it was mostly 'just' second degree burns. But once those blisters started popping and oozing puss all over my face, I was not a pretty sight. One of those referrals was a plastic surgeon, but the only real treatment I needed was bacitracin to prevent infection. All this happened just a couple weeks before graduation. Any open wounds had mostly healed in time, but the skin was still pretty tender, and I was supposed to keep out of the sun. So, I went everywhere with a wide brimmed hat, and avoided sitting out under the sun for all of the graduation rehearsals. I also avoided shaving, so I had that just wrong 17 year old level of stubble – more scruffy than rugged. A couple friends and I had also planned a cross country road trip right after graduation, which meant upgrading our provisional drivers licenses to full licenses, so we wouldn't have any restrictions driving during the trip. Oh man was that a horrible drivers license photo, between the scruff, red face, and completely unkempt hair once I took off the wide brimmed hat. Whenever anybody complained about a bad drivers license photo, I always had them beat (and they always agreed). Thankfully, I only developed a few minor scars, that weren't even that obvious when I was clean shaven, but are now completely hidden by my (adult) beard. Anyway, I was more careful adding shortening after that. I even got workman’s comp out of it.

Do pro-choice people at least think we should reduce the number of abortions? That's a weird question. It's about like asking if we should reduce the number of bypass surgeries for clogged arteries. On the one hand, as the old saying goes, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. It would be great if we could get people to live healthier lifestyles to avoid clogged arteries and the need for bypass surgeries in the first place. But as long as people do have clogged arteries, I very much want bypass surgery to be available. I don't want to reduce the number of bypass surgeries if the need still remains. And it still remains a fact of life that clogged arteries will happen regardless, so some amount of bypass surgeries will always be necessary. It's similar for abortion. It would be great if everybody had comprehensive sex education and easily available contraception and birth control to reduce the number of accidental pregnancies. And it would be great to have generally good living conditions for all families, easily affordable and accesible prenatal care, or at least adequate social safety nets, so that nobody was worried about having the means to raise a child with a good quality of life and opportunities. And it would be really great if there were no more rapes, developmental abnormalities, or other complications with pregnancies. So of course it would be nice to reduce all the reasons for abortions in the first place. But I don't want to reduce access to abortions while the need remains. And it's still a fact of life that some amount of abortions will always be necessary, because we never will fully eliminate all those reasons. So yes, like with any other healthcare issue, it would be best to reduce the causes that lead to needing medical intervention. But as long as the need's still there, you still provide the healthcare. And it's just a weird way to phrase a question, asking if we want to reduce a specific medical procedure, rather than addressing the causes that lead to that procedure.

What is the evolutionary reason for biological ageing? It's often helpful to think of evolution in terms of reproduction. As my one friends put it, "Forget survival of the fittest – the only reason survival is important in evolution is because you cannot reproduce when you're dead."* And while all things being equal, staying alive forever would certainly enable you to make more babies, all things aren't equal. Even if we didn't die of old age, something would end up killing us eventually – accidents, infections, predators, etc. Depending on the specific organism and its niche, there's some age by which it's overwhelmingly likely to be dead, anyway. On top of that, consider that maintaining a body doesn't come for free. It takes calories to repair injuries, maintain an immune system, suppress cancer, etc. And calories that are going towards that maintenance aren't going towards reproduction (mating, raising babies, defending territories, etc.). So, evolution finds a balance – put enough calories into maintenance to live long enough to reproduce, but just enough to maintain your body until the odds are likely that you'd be dead from something else, anyway. Since there's so little chance of any organisms within a certain species surviving past that age, it doesn't matter what happens to their bodies after that. You can see how this plays out by comparing the lifespans of different species. Something like a whale, which has very few natural predators, does have a very high likelihood of surviving year to year, so they have evolved to put significant energy into maintaining their bodies – over a century, in some cases. Same thing for large land tortoises on the Galapagos Islands. They do benefit by surviving for many breeding seasons, since it gives them that many more opportunities to reproduce. But something like a mouse, which is being hunted by everything from rattlesnakes to housecats to owls, isn't likely to last long in this world. Their best bet is to have as many offspring as quickly as they can, before something kills them, and not waste much energy on maintaining their bodies. Consequently, even if raised in captivity, mice won't live much past 1 to 3 years. Unlike some popular misconceptions might imply, it has nothing to do with gene turnover to promote evolution, or older generations making way for the next generation to avoid competing over resources (because honestly, from an evolutionary perspective, outside your own personal offspring, who gives a damn about the neighbor's kids – they're not carrying your genes**). It's because death is inevitable, so evolution finds the right balance of maintaining your body for long enough, and then putting everything else it can into reproduction. * That quote is from Scott Solomon, in his book, Future Humans: Inside the Science of Our Continuing Evolution: Solomon, Scott: 9780300208719: Amazon.com: Books ** Of course, that's oversimplifying things a bit. Kin selection does mean that it's beneficial to help relatives besides just your direct offspring. And various strategies of cooperation can be mutually beneficial even among non-related organisms. Still, it's never in an organism's evolutionary interests to sacrifice its own reproductive success for the sake of a non-relative.

Do atheists think that theists are unintelligent? It's complicated. So, let's get the provocative part out of the way, first. Numerous studies have found a negative correlation between intelligence and being religious. In other words, the less intelligent a person is, the more likely they are to be religious. And the more intelligent a person is, the more likely they are to be an atheist or agnostic. For example, one study that surveyed 432 people (The Relationship Between Religiousness/Spirituality and Psychometric Intelligence in the United States) found Christians to have an average IQ of 96.7, compared to 104.9 for atheists and 107.5 for agnostics. There was also a meta analysis (The Negative Intelligence–Religiosity Relation: New and Confirming Evidence) that synthesized the results of 83 prior studies, finding a negative correlation that ranged from -0.20 to -0.23. But, it's important to keep in mind that these are only averages, and that a correlation of -0.2 isn't very strong. Here are some examples of correlations, to give you an idea of what -0.2 looks like: SOURCE: https://quizlet.com/514729056/statistics-flash-cards/ As you might expect from the above, there's also quite a bit of overlap between religious and non-religious folks. If you were to plot bell curves of the IQs of those two groups, it would look something like this: SOURCE: Unwarranted Assumption There is lots of overlap, with plenty of religious folks among the most intelligent people, and plenty of non-religious folks that aren't the sharpest knives in the drawer. It's trivial to find examples of intelligent Christians (e.g. List of Christians in science and technology - Wikipedia). I follow plenty of intelligent Christians, myself, here on Quora. And, of course, there's plenty of discussion on just exactly what it means for non-believers to do better on IQ tests. Obviously, researchers try their best to account for confounding factors, but have they properly accounted for all of them? Is it general intelligence that makes the difference, specific types of intelligence, or even learned skillsets that allow some people to do better on these types of tests? But overall, there have been enough studies with similar results, that it's safe to say that non-believers are on average slightly more intelligent than believers. Still, the correlation is so small that it doesn't tell you much about individual believers or non-believers.

Why can't English rugby be as popular as American football in the USA? Well, they started off from the same roots, but then developed along independent paths in their respective countries. So it's no wonder that the version that developed in the USA is more popular in the USA. Both rugby and gridiron football, along with the various other types of football, grew out of a family of British games known as mob football, with different 'house rules' among every group in every town and village that played it. Since it was British colonists who were the first Europeans to come to what would become the U.S. and Canada, they brought along their British sports, including mob football. Round about the mid 1800s, social conditions were finally ripe to begin formalizing these diverse rules with different governing bodies. At the time, the Rugby School's rules were very similar to the rules at several American and Canadian colleges like Harvard, McGill, and Yale (in contrast to the association football rules of Cambridge and the Sheffield Football Club). The New World teams went on to develop new innovations that moved the sport further away from its cousin, rugby, including the line of scrimmage, a system of downs, and then in 1906 the forward pass (Walter Camp was especially influential in many of these innovations). ABOVE: An 1895 football game between Auburn and Georgia looking a lot more like rugby than modern day gridiron football SOURCE: College football - Wikipedia ABOVE: Another pre-forward pass college football game – the University of Minnesota vs. the University of Michigan in 1902 SOURCE: College football - Wikipedia So basically, the two sports started off largely the same, but then went down separate paths in each country. So of course the rules that developed in the USA are more popular here. If most Americans had wanted to play a game more similar to rugby, they wouldn't have changed the rules in the first place.

On what basis did evolutionists decide humans have a close common ancestry with apes, was it by looks? If so what about the kangaroo and the sloth? If by DNA, what about the banana? If it was by intelligence, what about the octopus? Carl Linnaeus is known as the father of modern taxonomy. He developed the now traditional system that you probably learned in high school biology – Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. This system is a nested hierarchy that we now recognize as being due to evolutionary relatedness, but Linaeus himself was a creationist (he died before Darwin was even born), and was merely trying to recognize the pattern of God's creation. And he based his system largely on physical similarity. Of course, he went deeper than superficial resemblances, and looked at the entire anatomy of organisms. That is how, for example, he recognized that dolphins and whales were mammals and not fish. And Linnaeus recognized the obvious anatomical similarities between humans and other apes, putting humans, chimpanzees, and orangutans all in the same genus, Homo (gorillas weren't yet known to European naturalists, or he almost surely would have included them, as well). I mean, the similarities between humans and other apes is sometimes so striking it's almost eerie: ABOVE SOURCE: Bonobo photos by Frans de Waal Kangaroos and sloths aren't nearly so anatomically similar to humans as the other apes. I mean, yes they're both mammals, so they're more related to humans than, say, a magpie or an oak tree, but not at that same level of similarity as the other apes. I mean, kangaroos are marsupials, for heaven's sake, with many, may differences to us placental mammals. Linnaeus recognized this over 200 years ago. DNA wasn't recognized as our hereditary molecule until the 1940s, and it's only been in more recent decades that scientists have been able to sequence DNA and otherwise study it in much more detail. Much like the anatomical comparisons that Linnaeus pioneered, you can also compare the similarity of the DNA of different organisms, and construct nested hierarchies of similarity. And when scientists did this, the resulting 'trees' matched up nearly spot on with the trees developed from traditional classification. In other words, while we knew from anatomical comparisons that humans were more closely related to apes than to sloths, DNA studies found exactly the same thing. So you have two different lines of evidence to do these comparisons, yet they produce essentially the same results. You mentioned bananas. Bananas are only distantly related to us people, and the genetics confirms this. While our DNA is roughly 98% the same with chimpanzees (it depends on how exactly you're doing the comparison), it's only around 50% the same with bananas. But bananas are multicellular eukaryotes, so even they are more closely related to us than some other life forms. Bacteria, for example, are even more distant relatives, with even less DNA in common with us. Your last question is about intelligence. The thing about lots of evolutionary traits is that they can develop separately through convergent evolution. When this happens, although the traits might have superficial resemblance, there will be lots of differences in the details. And octopuses and other cephalopods have brains that are very different from us mammals. They developed their intelligence through a completely different evolutionary path than us. So yes, anatomical similarities and genetic similarities are both used to determine the relatedness of organisms. But intelligence is a trait that can evolve independently, so it’s not as useful on its own.

Why are religious books deeper than novels? Aside from the point many other answers have made, that religious books aren't necessarily as profound as some religious folks like to claim, the other aspect is Sturgeon's Law – Ninety percent of everything is crap. You often see this discussed in relation to more recent art and literature. The reason people have rose colored glasses about music from the ‘60s, ‘70s, ‘80s, etc. is that we only still listen to the 10% of the stuff that was good, and the 90% that was crap was relegated to the dustbins of history, while we haven't yet filtered out the 90% of the crap that constitutes modern day music. The same goes for ancient mythology and scriptures. The books now assembled in the Old Testament weren't the only stories floating around in Israel and Judah at the time. They were just the most popular ones that scribes decided to compile. Same thing with the Gospels and other books of the New Testament. For examples, here are lists from Wikipedia of books that didn't make it into the Bible: So, the Bible represents the best of the best of religious writings from that culture.
